catalog_quote: The basic elements of Luganda tonology reveal a “2-3-2 system”, where H = high and L = low: (1) level of representation / tonal contrasts / description a. underlying input /H, Ø/ privative b. intermediate H, L, Ø ternary c. surface output H, L binary. As seen, the tonal representations depend on the level of representation. ... Although we show only H and L outputs, a restricted HL falling tone also exists (vs. LH rising, which the language prohibits), and a downstepped ↓H can result if one tone group ends with HL and the next begins with H. The tone-bearing unit is the mora. As seen in (2), Luganda words with an underlying /H/ obligatorily have a H to L pitch-drop: (2) ... b. 2σ /ki-kópo/ ki-kópò kì-kópò ‘cup’ /ki-sikí/ ki-sikî kì-sìkî ‘log’ c. 3σ /ki-sásilo/ ki-sásìlo kì-sásìló ‘rubbish’ /ki-yulífu/ ki-yulífù kì-yùlífù ‘torn’ (cl. 7) ... sweep_summary: Ganda (gand1255) is in the catalog as tonal on Hyman & Katamba 2010. Of the 10 sweep items, 6 are three works double-listed in Glottolog (H&K 2010 x2, Kalema 1977 x2, Hyman 1981 précis x2). Newly fetched sources and read: the ZASPiL DOI copy of H&K 2010 (silent on stress, tonal analysis, confirms) and Hyman's 1981 précis from SAL Supplement 8 (accentual analysis: at most one H-to-L drop per word, HL melody mapped by abstract accents; confirms, no stress claim). Read on file: Kalema 1977 (already listed), the only item with an explicit stress statement: 'no distinction in degrees of stress' (p. 136), accent = single lexically placed pitch drop, loanwords accented on the penult (p. 132); refines the catalog record with an explicit denial of stress but does not supersede the 2010 source. Not obtainable open: Tucker 1962 (JAL 1, print only; medium priority, unclear content), Hyman 1982 Globality (JLR, print only; low priority, the précis gives the gist), Philippson 1991 thesis (theses.fr 'accessible: non'; medium priority, ~30 East African Bantu languages on a tone-to-penult-stress cline, Luganda's treatment unknown). Fernald et al. 1989 is a Glottolog mis-attachment (infant-directed speech in six non-African varieties; not relevant). No catalog change indicated.

new_statements.quote: An approach such as the above, however, makes claims about Luganda phrases that cannot be fully substantiated, namely that the phrases such as the ones under investigation have segments with different degrees of stress. As far as we can tell, no distinction in degrees of stress exist in these phrases. What seems to be the case though is that once the pitch rises on the first accented segment, it remains high on all subsequent segments until after the right-most accented segment when it drops to low. [p. 136] — In Luganda, nouns of foreign origin seem to sub-divide themselves accentually into two categories depending on the type of structure the accented syllable has. In all cases, it is the last but one syllable that is accented [p. 132]
new_statements.citation: Kalema, John. 1977. Accent modification rules in Luganda. Studies in African Linguistics 8(2): 127-141.
new_statements.locator: p. 136 (discussion following (10)); p. 132 (loanwords); p. 130 (accent = single H-to-L fall per word)
new_statements.reading: Kalema (a native-speaker linguist at Makerere) explicitly denies that Luganda has degrees of stress; the only word-level prominence is the lexically placed H-to-L pitch drop ('accent' in the McCawley/Heny sense), one per word, which he treats as a pitch-accent stage feeding a tonal system. The lone positional rule is that loanwords take their H on the penultimate syllable (the likely source of Crabtree 1923's 'accent is on the penultimate' impression). This supports the catalog's TONAL coding and adds an explicit no-stress statement the 2010 source lacks (that source is silent on stress).

The secondary Crabtree carried quote is also verbatim (1923 ed. p. 15, fetched sources now). (2) Deciding source: a 2010 tonal-phonology article by the two leading Luganda prosodists; for a stress catalog the relevant fact — Luganda word prosody is lexical tone (privative /H, Ø/, mora TBU, one H-to-L drop per /H/ word), with no stress rule — is exactly what it documents. sources.note: Nothing: the word 'stress' does not occur in the paper (grep = 0 in both the Berkeley and the ZASPiL text); 'accent' appears only as the diacritic convention (acute = H, grave = L) and in the titles of Heny 1974 and Hyman 1982 in the references. The paper analyses Luganda word prosody as privative /H, Ø/ tone on moras with an obligatory H-to-L drop and phrase-level L insertion; it never posits stress.

sources.citation: Kalema, John. 1977. Accent modification rules in Luganda. Studies in African Linguistics 8(2): 127-141. [Glottolog 178727, title misspelt 'Lugnada'; already listed]
sources.quote: An approach such as the above, however, makes claims about Luganda phrases that cannot be fully substantiated, namely that the phrases such as the ones under investigation have segments with different degrees of stress. As far as we can tell, no distinction in degrees of stress exist in these phrases. What seems to be the case though is that once the pitch rises on the first accented segment, it remains high on all subsequent segments until after the right-most accented segment when it drops to low. (p. 136) — and p. 132, on loanwords: In Luganda, nouns of foreign origin seem to sub-divide themselves accentually into two categories depending on the type of structure the accented syllable has. In all cases, it is the last but one syllable that is accented
sources.locator: p. 136 (accent reduction, discussion of (10)); p. 132 (foreign nouns); p. 127 (abstract); p. 141 (conclusion)
sources.note: First-hand (Makerere) analysis. Luganda 'accent' = the location of the single H-to-L pitch drop per word (p. 130: 'there is just one fall in tone from high to low in each surface verb-word', quoting Heny 1970); it is lexically placed, not a fixed-position stress. Explicitly denies gradient stress: 'no distinction in degrees of stress' in phrases (p. 136). Luganda is 'a pitch accent language up to some point' then tonal (abstract p. 127, conclusion p. 141). The only positional regularity stated is for loanwords, where the accent (H) falls on the penultimate syllable (p. 132).

sources.citation: Crabtree, William A. 1923. Elements of Luganda grammar, together with exercises and vocabulary. Kampala: Uganda Bookshop / London: SPCK (archive.org elementsoflugand00crabuoft).
sources.quote: p.15 carried quote confirmed verbatim. p.174 gives Crabtree's actual rule: 'ACCENT. Usually on the Penultimate of the Root... iii. The Root is monosyllabic and a. Enclitic... The Accent though not on the root returns to the Penult. b. Accented. The word is oxytone, e.g. omuti, a tree', plus a separate 'Intonation or Tone Accent. Often on the a final of Verbs... In some cases it would seem as though the Tone Accent exceeded in intensity the True Accent.' I.e. a root-based, lexically variable 'accent' heard alongside tone by a missionary ear, not a word-penult stress rule.

sources.citation: Cole, Desmond T. 1965. Some features of Ganda linguistic structure, Parts 1-3. African Studies 24: 3-54, 71-116, 199-240 (ERIC reprints NDEA-VI-205-1/2/3; = Cole 1967, Witwatersrand UP).
sources.quote: 'Ganda has two tonemes or phonemes of tone, High (H) and Low (L)... The substrate (segmental) unit of tonal placement or accommodation is the syllable, each syllable having a capacity, according to type, of one or two tonemes... Tonal clusters may be HH, LL or HL, apparently never *LH.' The word 'stress' occurs zero times in all three parts (scanned grep).

sources.citation: Hyman, Larry M. 1981. An autosegmental accentual account of Luganda tone. In Précis from the 12th Conference on African Linguistics (Studies in African Linguistics, Supplement 8), 64-68. [Glottolog 179064, title misspelt 'Lugnada'; Hyman's 2021 CV lists it under 1982 as '13th Annual Conference']
sources.quote: I. The Luganda Surface System: As evident from Cole, Meeussen, Stevick, Heny, and McCawley and others, there is at most one drop from H to L per word. In fact, one needs at least the following information to predict melody: 1. Place where rise occurs, if any 2. Place where fall occurs, if any 3. Nature of the L tones following the H tones, if any (p. 64) [...] I shall take the position that there is a constant "accentual melody" HL in Luganda and that the initial L is a boundary tone. (p. 66)
sources.note: No stress claim. 'Accent' is an abstract asterisk on vowels that governs where the HL melody maps; the word-level fact is culminativity of the H-to-L drop (at most one per word), lexically placed (e.g. o-mu-tí 'tree' with final accent vs. stem-accented verbs). This is the accentual analysis that Hyman later replaced by the privative /H, Ø/ tonal analysis of Hyman & Katamba 2010.

sources.quote: Ces systèmes varient en effet depuis des langues pleinement tonales (kikuyu) jusqu'à des langues à accent démarcatif pénultième (swahili), tous les cas intermédiaires étant représentés. [...] Une trentaine de langues en tout sont utilisées comme exemples. Enfin, on établit systématiquement les correspondances prosodiques entre chacune des langues concernées et le bantu commun et on propose l'hypothèse que le moteur principal de l'évolution des systèmes concernes a été l'émergence d'un accent démarcatif sur la pénultième servant de limite de domaine pour l'association tonale. — Translation: These systems range from fully tonal languages (Kikuyu) to languages with a demarcative penultimate accent (Swahili), with all intermediate cases represented. [...] Some thirty languages in all are used as examples. Finally, prosodic correspondences between each language and Common Bantu are established systematically, and the hypothesis is put forward that the main driver of the evolution of these systems was the emergence of a demarcative accent on the penult serving as the domain limit for tone association.
sources.note: Abstract only: a comparative typology of East African Bantu tone/accent systems on a tonal-to-penultimate-stress cline, ~30 languages. Whether Luganda is one of the sample languages and how it is classified cannot be determined from the abstract; the full text is not online (theses.fr: accessible = non; HAL query returns 0).
